best_for: Amateur astronomers who plan observing nights on a laptop, and astrophotographers who want free software to run their mount, camera and guider.

points.title: A planetarium that is free
points.text: KStars is free under the GPL and shows up to 100 million stars, about 10,000 deep-sky objects, planets, comets and asteroids. You can speed up or slow down the sky to see what will be up later tonight.

points.title: Planning tools come with it
points.text: An observation planner and calculator tools predict conjunctions and plot planet positions over time. That saves you from juggling a separate almanac while you plan a session.

points.title: Ekos runs the whole rig
points.text: Ekos, built into KStars, controls telescopes, cameras, focusers, filter wheels and domes through the INDI library, and handles alignment, guiding, focusing and capture. The 3.8.5 release added fixes to the AI guider and scheduler.

points.title: Device control is strongest on Linux
points.text: KStars's device page says native INDI support gives full control of your instruments under Linux. The project's Windows and macOS pages do not say how hardware control works there, so check before you build a Windows imaging rig around it.

points.title: macOS has two builds
points.text: There are separate Apple Silicon and Intel disk images; a universal build is only planned. The stated minimum macOS differs between pages, and readers of the 3.8.5 release post reported it would not install on Big Sur, so expect to need a recent macOS.

points.title: Windows and Linux installs
points.text: Windows 10 or later is required, and the Windows installer comes in per-user and machine-wide forms. The Flatpak is verified on Flathub as published by KDE, and the release post recommends it for Linux.

points.title: Versions kept here
points.text: The Windows listing keeps 11 versions. macOS and Linux list only the current release, so downgrades there need another source.
